2026-08-18: the plugin was renamed sdlc → mmo after this walkthrough was recorded. Commands and screenshots below (/sdlc-run, SDLC_SELECT) are shown as they were at the time.

The same run, through the agent door — what it costs to route Gemini as an agent.

The install asks one question: should Gemini work as a model, or as an agent inside the folder? This run answered “as an agent”. Everything else is held constant — same plugin, same opus-plus-flash policy, same brief, same four human gates. Thirteen frames from that run in order, then two of the files it left on disk, with every figure reconciled against the run record rather than the screen.

2As an agent (Antigravity SDK)  — the one choice the install asks for

The run, frame by frame

Timestamps are from the screenshots themselves. The chip on each frame says which tier was working at that moment — the premium tier judging, the mechanical tier building as an agent, or the human at a gate.

01
6:55:38 AM
Human

The one question the install asks

Setup is one sentence with a repo URL — the same install as on any other machine. It ends by asking exactly one thing: should Gemini work as a model or as an agent? Option 1 sends the code over and gets text back, one request per task. Option 2 hands Gemini the working directory and lets it run commands and edit files itself. The card says out loud that option 2 “costs several times more per task”. This run chose option 2.

The credential side is never a question. The install detects what is on the machine and reports it. The agent question appears at all only because Vertex ADC was found — the agent worker builds its client with vertex=True and has no API-key branch, so on an AI-Studio-key-only machine this question is skipped entirely.
02
7:10:30 AM
Human

What this machine actually had

Credentials are reported, not requested. Vertex AI via ADC on project ai-studies-console; no ANTHROPIC_API_KEY, which changes nothing about whether the run works and everything about whether the premium tier's tokens are vendor-billed or estimated. The install also worked around a broken Homebrew Python by fetching a standalone 3.12 for the worker's virtualenv, and flagged that Claude Code had overwritten its own settings file mid-install — with the one-line command to re-apply it.

The agent path needs a new Claude Code session. Plugin MCP servers start at session start, so a run launched inside the setup session would not fail — it would quietly execute every phase on the premium model and hand over a bill several times what the policy promises, which is the one outcome this plugin exists to prevent.
03
7:11:39 AM
Opus

/sdlc-run states which door it is on

Before asking for anything, the orchestrator re-runs its own setup check and reports where it stands. SDLC_SELECT=gemini-flash=flash-agsdk-worker — the slot=option form; a bare leaf name is rejected at policy load. It names the consequence in the same breath: the mechanical tier is reached as an Antigravity agent working in the folder, not as a single model call. “I'll come back to what that costs.”

04
7:12:20 AM
Opus

The policy, and the warning that came true

The rate card is not changed by the door: Opus at $5.00 in / $0.50 cached / $25.00 out per million, gemini-3.5-flash at $1.50 / $0.15 / $9.00. What changes is the token count, because an agent re-sends its conversation on every tool call. That is stated before any money is spent, along with the receipts it will leave behind: a delegation/ directory beside the telemetry holding the brief each worker was given and a receipt for what it did.

“One thing pre-flight cannot check.” It constructs the agent's adapter but never calls it, so entitlement, region and credential validity all stay unknown until the first delegated packet — which lands after requirements, design and task planning have already been billed to Opus. Pre-flight's typist probe covers this: every run passes probe_typists, which sends one minimal call through each typist the run types with, the agent door's included, so a refused entitlement or credential stops the run at its start, for cents, before any phase is billed.
05
7:12:51 AM
Flash · agent

A two-cent probe, and the shape of the problem

Rather than discover a broken agent path an hour in, the orchestrator offers one trivial delegation first. It exits 0 for $0.020130 and confirms that project and region dispatch, bill and price correctly. The number worth reading is the one beside it: 12,250 input tokens for a one-word answer. That is the per-turn preamble, measured, before the run has started.

06
7:17:02 AM
Human

Gate 1 — requirements, with the judgment calls named

14 functional requirements across three modules, 10 non-functional, 8 acceptance criteria, an empty-by-design PII inventory. The gate does not ask for a rubber stamp: it surfaces the three places the brief was silent and the model had to decide — 404 rather than 405 on a wrong method, the app/listen() split, the PORT override — and offers each one back as a revision. Spent so far: $0.1229.

07
7:23:03 AM
Human

Gate 2 — design, and three things the architect caught

Five ADRs, a five-file flat tree, and an explicit list of what will not be generated so codegen does not invent it. ADR-004 is a real bug avoided: express is pinned at ^5.1.0, and under path-to-regexp v8 a bare app.all('*', ...) throws TypeError: Missing parameter name at module load — the whole suite would fail on require('./app') with an error that looks nothing like a routing bug. Test strategy moved to three cases, not two. Cost so far $0.4263, both phases judgment-tier.

08
7:30:59 AM
Flash · agent

The receipts, on disk, mid-run

Every delegated packet writes three files into .sdlc/delegation/: the brief the worker was handed, a usage sidecar, and a receipt for what it did. This is the directory partway through the run, four packets in. The extra spend the agent door incurs is inspectable rather than merely asserted.

09
7:58:26 AM
Flash · agent

“The mechanical tier is not behaving as the cheap tier”

Codegen finishes and the orchestrator raises the finding immediately rather than saving it for the report: $0.6330 across five packets against $0.5507 for the three judgment phases. It names the cause — each agent session reads its own files, runs npm install and npm test itself, and burns reasoning tokens — and it names the counterfactual: through the completion door those same five packets would have been a small fraction of this.

The interim figure on screen calls tp_codegen_002 a 24-line file; the reconciled final report says 28 lines. The cost, $0.262851, is the same number in both.
10
8:19:24 AM
Human

Gate 3 — a security review that ran the code

PASS WITH ACCEPTED RISKS: zero defects at every severity, two info notes about layers below the application, npm audit clean across 347 packages. The reviewer verified by execution rather than by reading — it copied app.js, injected four throwing routes above the catch-all, and re-ran the 500 path under unset / development / production to show the protection is structural, not environment-dependent. 23 live HTTP probes plus 10 raw-socket malformed-wire probes.

8:26:51 AM
Opus

Eleven rows, $2.182165

The per-phase table, straight from the telemetry. It also declares its own waste: a duplicate senior review costing $0.206177, because the first dispatch was backgrounded and its artifact was not visible to the orchestrator before it re-dispatched. Both attempts independently returned approve_with_nits with zero code defects. Without the duplicate the run would have cost $1.975988.

Flash · agent

Per packet — where the money actually went

tp_codegen_002 cost $0.262851 for a 28-line file — more than all of requirements analysis, more than all of task planning, about as much as both combined. Cost tracks session length, not artifact size: two packets producing comparable artifacts (397 vs 459 bytes) differ 5.7× because the second ran npm install itself and then accrued 379,548 cached input tokens re-reading its workspace. 77% of mechanical output tokens were reasoning rather than content; the docs packet hit 92%.

13
8:27:49 AM
Opus

Two things worth knowing

The routing was not the problem. It fired correctly on every packet and the debug escalation never triggered — the leaf was the cost lever, not the policy, and the same policy against flash-completion would isolate that directly. The duplicate review was a timing bug rather than a model failure, and re-running synchronously instead of fabricating a verdict was the right call at $0.206177. Four open items are recorded as structured entries, every one carrying code_change_required: false.

Inside one packet

Every row in that table left three files behind — the brief, the usage sidecar and the receipt. These are two of the three for tp_codegen_002, the most expensive packet of the run, read straight off disk after it finished. Nothing here is reconstructed; it is what the run wrote.

A
tp_codegen_002
Flash · agent

The brief the agent was handed — worker-task-tp_codegen_002.md

An agent session is not given a prompt string; it is given a place to work and a job. The brief names the working directory and says plainly that nothing outside it is reachable, then gives one instruction and excerpts — not whole files — from design.md, with real paths so the agent can open the rest itself if it needs to.

The instruction carries ADR-004 forward as an explicit prohibition: no bare app.all('*', ...), and the terminal error handler must declare all four parameters because Express identifies error middleware solely by fn.length === 4. The design phase found the trap; the brief is how the mechanical tier inherits it.
B
tp_codegen_002
Flash · agent

The receipt it left behind — worker-usage-tp_codegen_002.json

The usage sidecar for the same packet, and the clearest single view of what the agent door costs. 464,291 input tokens — 379,548 of them cached — plus 3,766 tokens of content and 4,990 of reasoning, to produce a 28-line file. thinking is set to NONE; the 4,990 reasoning tokens are what the agent loop spends anyway, not something the policy asked for. This sidecar was written by SDK 0.1.9, which counts the cached tokens inside prompt_token_count; SDK 0.1.16 counts them on top of it, and the plugin reads each sidecar by the SDK version recorded in it.

Below the usage block, all 19 tool calls are recorded with their arguments and resolved paths: 8 run_command, 4 list_directory, 4 edit_file, 2 view_file, 1 find_file. The eight shell commands are the agent installing dependencies and running the suite itself — work the completion door never does, and the reason this packet cost $0.262851.
